An RL-Fine-Tuned VLA for Humanoid Manipulation, From My Own Phone Videos
Open challenge submission · Unitree G1 + Dex3-1 in MuJoCo · SmolVLA · MediaPipe · models published on Hugging Face
Oct 2026
In progress
Done: 26 phone clips of my own hand retargeted onto a G1 with a three-fingered hand, 584 demos, a SmolVLA fine-tune improved by RL on its own rollouts, and an evaluation at 52% on 60 unseen block poses from cameras alone, with 0 falls — benchmarked against a motion-planner pipeline at 73%. Next: correction data at the grasp, which is where the remaining failures are.
The brief was that my own data has to drive the robot. So I filmed myself 26 times picking up a block and standing it on a star, tracked my hand with MediaPipe, and turned my hand's path — where it goes, how it turns, when it closes and opens, and how fast — into motion for a Unitree G1 with a Dex3-1 hand in MuJoCo. Those replays become demonstrations, the demonstrations fine-tune SmolVLA, and the VLA is then improved with reinforcement learning on its own rollouts.

Two choices shaped everything. First, the VLA outputs a hand pose in the table frame, not joint angles. The robot stands on its own legs and its pelvis sways several centimetres whenever the arm moves, so a joint-space action means something different depending on how the body has drifted; a grasp-centre pose means the same thing always, and IK from the current torso pose turns it into joints. Second, the block is held by contact and friction only — no welds, no attachment constraints. That makes the grasp a real physical event that can fail, and most of the remaining failures are exactly that.

The VLA is never told where the block is. It has to find it in the camera images.

Setup
A humanoid at a table is not a fixed-base arm. Every arm motion pushes the body, so the legs are part of the manipulation problem.
Robot
Unitree G1, 29 DoF with a full floating base, in MuJoCo 3.15. Unitree Dex3-1 three-fingered hand (7 DoF) on the right arm; the left arm holds its rest pose.
Task & Success
Pick up a 3.5 × 3.5 × 8 cm, 80 g standing block and stand it upright on a star. Success requires the block upright within 3 cm, the robot still standing, and no part of the robot except the hand touching the table.
My Data
26 phone clips at 4K/60 fps, filmed at eye level, plus ChArUco calibration video. ArUco markers give the table frame. Camera calibration came out at 1.31 px RMS. 18 of the 26 clips yield a usable hand track.
Perception
MediaPipe's 21 hand landmarks → the pinch point (thumb-tip / index-tip midpoint) in 3-D, hand yaw, grip aperture, and the grasp / release moments detected from when the block starts and stops moving. Monocular depth from MediaPipe's metric hand model plus PnP, one scale per clip.
Policy
SmolVLA 450M fine-tuned from lerobot/smolvla_base. Inputs: head camera, wrist camera, the hand state, and the text instruction. Output: chunks of 5-D hand-pose actions, re-planned every 5 steps (0.2 s).
Compute
One 8 GB RTX 4060 laptop GPU for everything — the leg policy, every SmolVLA fine-tune and every RL round.
The Legs Are Their Own RL Problem
Before any manipulation can be learned, the robot has to hold still while something else moves its arms.
01 A stance policy trained to be disturbed by its own arms. PPO in mjlab across 4096 parallel environments, with stand-only commands, table-work postures, and random arm motions injected during training — 70% of the right arm's reach goals being palm-in grasp poses like the ones the task actually needs. Rewards weight standing-still terms heavily. The leg policy also sees the arm targets, so it can anticipate the push rather than only react to it.
02 Measured, not assumed: the workspace is limited by the arm, not by balance. I moved the grasp centre to every point of a 5 cm grid on the table and held it for 3 s. Across all 66 points the feet never moved more than 1.1 cm and the robot never fell. What changes across the grid is how much the pelvis sways to counterbalance — which is precisely why the actions are hand poses in the table frame rather than joint angles.
03 A physics bug found by measuring a grip that should have held. With MuJoCo's default pyramidal friction cone a block slowly crept out of a 76 N grip. Switching to the elliptic cone with impratio 10 and a 5 ms step fixed it. Had I not checked, every grasp failure afterwards would have been blamed on the policy.
Every Iteration, on the Same 60 Unseen Block Poses
Seed 123 throughout. A model is kept only if it beats its parent on the full 60-pose evaluation, otherwise it is rolled back.

n = 60 gives roughly ±6% at one standard deviation, so each ~8-point gain is about 1.3 SD — real, but not large. Being explicit about that is the point of re-running all 60 poses every time rather than reporting the best few. Three of five RL rounds were rolled back, which is what the keep-only-if-it-beats-its-parent rule is for.
Why a Wrist Camera · Measuring Where the Policy Fails
After three RL rounds plateaued, I stopped tuning and measured the error at the moment the fingers close. 198 rollouts.
Grasp-centre error when the grip closesRolloutsLifted
< 1 cm26◆ 81%
1–2 cm4466%
2–4 cm8643%
That is the whole story in one table: the policy is not failing to understand the task, it is failing to place its fingers. In the 224 px head image the block is about 14 px wide — 1 cm is roughly 4 px — and the hand covers half of it at exactly the moment precision matters. RL can only re-weight what the policy can see, so no amount of further RL on the head camera was going to fix this. Adding a wrist camera took lift from 55% to 67% and success from 45% to 52%.

The benchmark wins by about 25 points, and I am reporting it that way deliberately. A motion planner produces perfectly consistent demonstrations; my own hand varies from clip to clip and is noisier, and that noise costs real performance. But the planner version does not meet the brief — its arm motion is not mine. Keeping both, on identical poses, is what makes the cost of the constraint measurable instead of a matter of opinion.
How the RL Works
SmolVLA is a flow-matching policy, so ordinary policy gradients are the wrong tool.
01 Advantage-weighted resampling, not policy gradient. Following Larchenko et al.'s Learning to Fold: a policy-gradient update pushes the action chunk off the narrow manifold of valid actions, whereas re-weighting the data sampler only changes how often the policy sees actions it already produces. The loss stays plain flow matching and the LeRobot training loop is untouched.
02 An empirical stage value instead of a learned critic. Every rollout frame is labelled with a privileged progress stage — hand at the grasp point, lifted, over the star, placed. The value of stage k is simply P(success | reached k), measured from the rollouts, and a frame's advantage is the step up it achieved. Frames are then sampled ∝ exp(A). On one laptop GPU that is far cheaper than training a value network, and there is nothing to diverge.
03 Extra negative credit for the second before the block topples. Knocking the block over is the failure that a success-only signal notices far too late.
What Did Not Work
Reported because each one changed the design, and because a result with no failures listed is usually a result that was not examined.
01 The first demo set succeeded only 34% of the time in simulation. Traced step by step: the 0.6× scaled carry lifted the block only 0.5–3 cm, fast approaches knocked it over, and the hand oscillated above the star. Adding a straight 14 cm descent with a pause to close, and a settle before release, raised it to 64%. A stronger squeeze made it worse, which is the opposite of the obvious fix.
02 BC v0 scoring 0% was a bug, not a learning failure. The planned segments stored the planner's final goal as the action. Replaying known-good demos through the evaluation controller also gave 0/6 — which is what proved it was the interface and not the model, and is a much faster check than retraining.
03 Doubling the demonstrations did nothing. 572 → 1151 head-camera demos moved success from 45% to 42%. More of the same data does not fix a perception limit.
04 The wrist camera alone did not help at first (43%). My demonstrations never show a correction — "the hand is 3 cm off, move it" — because the scripted grasp uses the true block pose and so is never wrong. The camera only paid off once RL had rollouts to re-weight. That is what points at DAgger-style correction data as the next step rather than more RL.
05 Blocks lying on their side are not handled. 10 of my 26 clips show this; the Dex3 would need an arm pose extreme enough to make the legs step.
Next Steps
All aimed at the grasp, and at making more of each demonstration come from me rather than from a script.
01 Record recoveries. Clips where the block slips from my hand and I pick it up again, retargeted through the whole recovery, so the VLA sees how a bad grasp gets corrected instead of only clean ones.
02 A wrist camera on my own hand while filming. The robot's wrist camera gave the single biggest gain; a matching view in the human data would supply it from my recordings rather than only from simulation.
03 Replace the scripted grasp and place with my own motion. With the two above, my motion can cover the last 14 cm and the placement too — taking the demonstrations from 54% mine to 100% mine. IK stays, because it only converts a hand pose into joint angles.
My contribution
All of it: filming and calibrating the 26 clips, the MediaPipe hand-tracking and monocular-depth pipeline, the retargeting from my pinch path to the robot's grasp centre, the MuJoCo scene and contact tuning, the RL stance policy for legs and waist, the workspace characterisation, the SmolVLA fine-tunes, the advantage-weighted RL loop with its empirical stage values, the planner/IK benchmark, and the evaluation harness.
Upstream
SmolVLA and LeRobot (Hugging Face); mjlab for the leg-policy training; MuJoCo Menagerie for the G1 and Dex3-1 models; MediaPipe for hand landmarks. The AWR-through-the-sampler idea is from Larchenko et al., Learning to Fold (arXiv 2606.27163); I reimplemented the sampler and substituted an empirical stage value for their learned one.
